category: VSM generators, EasyHDL, interactive debugging and simulation options
description: The individual generator types (analogue DC/Sine/Pulse/Exp/SFFM/PWLIN/File/Audio, digital DState/DEdge/DPulse/DClock/DPattern and scripted EasyHDL generators), the newer instruments (System Scope, CAN Bus Analyser), the Debug-menu commands and windows used while an interactive simulation is paused (timed breakpoints, animated single step, active popups, watchpoints, real-time hardware breakpoints, diagnostics, popup and persistent-data resets), the Animation Options and Simulator Options settings that control speed and SPICE accuracy, and the graph-editing commands used in graph-based analysis.

tools.name: DC generator
tools.description: The simplest analogue generator: a constant voltage (or current) source placed in Generator Mode and wired to a net. It supplies bias and reference levels in graph-based analyses and interactive simulation, and its value can be a swept variable name (e.g. X) for DC Sweep graphs.
tools.usage: Generator Mode > 'DC' > place on a wire > edit: Voltage (Volts) or tick 'Current Source' and enter Amps

parameters.name: Voltage / Current
parameters.description: Fixed level; may be an expression or sweep variable.

parameters.name: Current Source
parameters.description: Switches the generator to a current source.

tools.example: Place a DC generator named VIN = 2.5 on the op-amp input and run a DC Transfer Curve graph sweeping it from 0 to 5V.
tools.notes: Generators referenced to ground by default; untick 'Isolate Before?' to keep an existing connection on the wire.

tools.name: Sine generator
tools.description: Sinusoidal source defined by amplitude (peak, RMS or peak-to-peak), frequency (or period), DC offset, start delay and an optional damping factor, matching the SPICE SIN source. It is the reference input for Frequency, Distortion, Noise and Fourier graphs and the usual stimulus for amplifier and filter tests.
tools.usage: Generator Mode > 'Sine' > edit: Offset (Volts), Amplitude (Volts) / RMS / Peak-Peak, Frequency (Hz) or Period, Delay (Secs), Damping Factor (1/s)

parameters.name: Amplitude
parameters.description: Entered as peak, RMS or peak-to-peak.

parameters.name: Frequency / Period
parameters.description: Either form accepted, with SI suffixes.

parameters.name: Delay / Damping Factor
parameters.description: Start delay and exponential decay of the envelope.

tools.example: 1kHz 100mV sine into a common-emitter amplifier; Analogue graph of input and output, then a Fourier graph to read THD.
tools.notes: For frequency analysis the sine generator is dragged onto the Frequency graph as the reference; its amplitude is ignored there (small-signal).

tools.name: Pulse generator
tools.description: Analogue pulse train (SPICE PULSE): initial (low) and pulsed (high) voltages, start time, rise and fall times, pulse width (or duty cycle) and frequency/period. It produces clocks, square waves and step stimuli for transient analysis; with negative polarity and a single pulse it doubles as a button-press stimulus in graph-based MCU simulations where the user cannot click.
tools.usage: Generator Mode > 'Pulse' > edit: Initial (Low) Voltage, Pulsed (High) Voltage, Start (Secs), Rise Time, Fall Time, Pulse Width / Pulse Width (%), Frequency / Period

parameters.name: Initial / Pulsed voltage
parameters.description: Low and high levels.

parameters.name: Rise / Fall Time
parameters.description: Edge times; keep non-zero for convergence.

parameters.name: Pulse Width / Frequency
parameters.description: Width as time or % duty, repetition as frequency or period.

tools.example: 0-5V, 1kHz, 50% pulse into an RC low-pass; Analogue graph shows the exponential charging edges.
tools.notes: Digital pulse stimuli for logic pins are better made with DPulse/DClock so the digital simulator handles them natively.

tools.name: Exponent (EXP) generator
tools.description: SPICE EXP source producing a single exponential rise followed by an exponential fall: initial and pulsed voltage, rise start time and rise time constant, fall start time and fall time constant. It models capacitor charge/discharge style stimuli and impulse-like excitations for transient tests.
tools.usage: Generator Mode > 'Exp' > edit: Initial (Low) Voltage, Pulsed (High) Voltage, Rise Start Time, Rise Time Constant, Fall Start Time, Fall Time Constant

parameters.name: Rise/Fall start time
parameters.description: When each exponential segment begins.

parameters.name: Rise/Fall time constant
parameters.description: Tau of each segment.

tools.example: Model a decaying supply glitch: 5V to 3V with a 1us fall constant at 2ms, back to 5V with 100us rise constant at 2.5ms, and check the brown-out comparator response.
tools.notes: Use PWLIN for arbitrary multi-segment shapes.

tools.name: SFFM (single-frequency FM) generator
tools.description: SPICE SFFM source: a carrier sine frequency-modulated by a second sine, defined by offset, amplitude, carrier frequency, modulation index and signal (modulating) frequency. It is used to test FM demodulators, PLLs and filter behaviour under modulated input.
tools.usage: Generator Mode > 'SFFM' > edit: Offset, Amplitude, Carrier Frequency, Modulation Index, Signal Frequency

parameters.name: Carrier Frequency
parameters.description: fc of the carrier sine.

parameters.name: Modulation Index / Signal Frequency
parameters.description: Depth and rate of the modulation.

tools.example: 100kHz carrier, 1kHz modulating tone, index 5 into an LM566/PLL demodulator; Fourier graph shows the sidebands.
tools.notes: Amplitude modulation is not a generator type - build AM with an EasyHDL script or a multiplier circuit.

tools.name: Piecewise Linear (PWLIN) generator
tools.description: Defines an arbitrary analogue waveform as a list of (time, voltage) points joined by straight segments, either typed into the table or drawn graphically in the generator's editor. It reproduces measured waveforms, multi-level test vectors and any stimulus too complex for the Pulse/Exp sources; a minimum rise/fall time property prevents zero-time steps.
tools.usage: Generator Mode > 'Pwlin' > edit: add Time/Voltage pairs in the grid or drag points on the graphical editor; set Outside Range behaviour and Minimum Rise/Fall Time

parameters.name: Time / Voltage points
parameters.description: Ordered pairs defining the waveform.

parameters.name: Minimum rise/fall time
parameters.description: Applied where consecutive points share a time.

parameters.name: Scaling
parameters.description: Time and voltage multipliers for the whole table.

tools.example: Reproduce a captured ECG shape as 40 points and feed it to an instrumentation-amplifier front end for an Analogue graph.
tools.notes: Beyond the last point the output holds the last value (or repeats, depending on the option chosen). For long recordings use the File generator instead.

tools.name: File generator
tools.description: Plays back a waveform stored in an ASCII data file of time/value pairs, so a measurement exported from an oscilloscope, a MATLAB/Python-generated stimulus or a previous Proteus graph export can drive the circuit. It complements the Tape Recorder instrument, which records simulation results in a form this generator can replay.
tools.usage: Generator Mode > 'File' > edit: Data File = path to the .dat text file (two columns: time, value)

parameters.name: Data File
parameters.description: Text file with whitespace-separated time and voltage columns.

tools.example: Export the output of one design's graph to a file, then use a File generator in a second design to feed the recorded waveform into the next stage.
tools.notes: Points are interpolated linearly; very large files slow the transient setup.

tools.name: Audio generator
tools.description: Uses a Windows WAV file as the stimulus, converting the samples to a voltage waveform with selectable amplitude, DC offset and channel (mono/left/right), so audio circuits (filters, amplifiers, codecs, MCU audio processing) can be driven with real music or speech. Paired with an Audio graph, the simulated output can be played back through the PC sound card.
tools.usage: Generator Mode > 'Audio' > edit: WAV File, Amplitude (peak), DC Offset, Channel

parameters.name: WAV File
parameters.description: PCM WAV source; long files increase simulation time proportionally.

parameters.name: Amplitude / Offset
parameters.description: Scales the normalised samples into volts.

tools.example: Feed a 2-second speech WAV into a 3-band tone-control circuit and listen to the result from an Audio graph of the output.
tools.notes: Requires the Advanced Simulation Features module for the Audio graph playback.

tools.name: DState (digital state) generator
tools.description: Digital generator that holds a fixed logic state - strong high, strong low, weak high/low, floating or a specified custom level - for the whole simulation. It ties inputs to constant levels (mode-select pins, chip enables, unused inputs) without needing a power terminal and resistor, and its weak states let pull-up/pull-down contention be tested.
tools.usage: Generator Mode > 'DState' > edit: State = Strong High / Strong Low / Weak High / Weak Low / Floating / Custom

parameters.name: State
parameters.description: Logic level and drive strength.

tools.example: Tie a 74HC595's OE low and SRCLR high with two DState generators instead of power terminals.
tools.notes: Digital generators output logic states to the DSIM simulator; when connected to an analogue net an interface model converts them to voltages automatically.

tools.name: DEdge (digital edge) generator
tools.description: Produces a single logic transition - rising or falling - at a specified time, holding the initial state before and the final state after. It is the digital equivalent of a step input, used to trigger one-shots, reset sequences or to release an MCU reset at a chosen instant in a graph-based run.
tools.usage: Generator Mode > 'DEdge' > edit: Edge Polarity (Positive/Negative), Edge At (Secs)

parameters.name: Edge At
parameters.description: Time of the transition.

parameters.name: Polarity
parameters.description: Low-to-high or high-to-low.

tools.example: Hold MCLR low and release it with a positive DEdge at 10ms to see the firmware's start-up sequence on a Digital graph.
tools.notes: For repeated edges use DClock or DPattern.

tools.name: DPulse (digital pulse) generator
tools.description: Single digital pulse of chosen polarity: start time and either pulse width or stop time. It is the standard way to inject a button press or strobe into a graph-based simulation of a microcontroller (where you cannot click), or to test one-shot and edge-detection logic.
tools.usage: Generator Mode > 'DPulse' > edit: Pulse Polarity (Positive/Negative Pulse), Start Time, Pulse Width or Stop Time

parameters.name: Polarity
parameters.description: Positive (low-high-low) or negative (high-low-high) pulse.

parameters.name: Start Time / Pulse Width
parameters.description: When and how long.

tools.example: In the Getting Started I2C graph tutorial a negative DPulse at 1.25s, 50ms wide, on RD2 represents the mode button press that starts temperature polling.
tools.notes: The wire's pull-up terminal may need moving to make room for the generator on the net.

tools.name: DClock (digital clock) generator
tools.description: Continuous digital square wave defined by clock type (low-high-low or high-low-high), the time of the first edge and frequency or period. It clocks counters, shift registers and flip-flops in logic simulations and provides external clocks to processor models or peripherals that take a pin clock.
tools.usage: Generator Mode > 'DClock' > edit: Clock Type (Low-High-Low / High-Low-High Clock), First Edge At, Timing: Frequency (Hz) or Period (Secs)

parameters.name: Clock Type
parameters.description: Initial level and first-edge direction.

parameters.name: First Edge At
parameters.description: Delay before the clock starts.

parameters.name: Frequency / Period
parameters.description: 50% duty square wave.

tools.example: 1MHz DClock into a 74HC4040 12-bit counter; Digital graph of Q0-Q11 confirms the ripple delays.
tools.notes: For non-50% duty cycles use DPattern or a Pulse generator.

tools.name: DPattern (digital pattern) generator
tools.description: Arbitrary digital bit stream: an initial state, the time of the first edge, a bit timing (equal mark/space from a frequency/period or explicit pulse widths) and the pattern itself, either a continuous sequence of pulses or a specific bit string (e.g. '01101100') that can repeat or stop. It is used for serial protocol stimuli, key-bounce emulation and test vectors for combinational logic.
tools.usage: Generator Mode > 'DPattern' > edit: Initial State, First Edge At, Timing (Equal Mark/Space or Specific Pulse Width), Transitions (Continuous Sequence of Pulses / Specific pulse train), Bit Pattern string

parameters.name: Bit Pattern
parameters.description: String of 0/1 characters played at the bit rate.

parameters.name: Repeat
parameters.description: Loop the pattern or hold the last bit.

tools.example: Bit pattern '1010101011111111' at 9600 bit/s into a UART RX pin emulates two received bytes for an ISR test in a Digital graph.
tools.notes: For long or conditional sequences use an EasyHDL scripted generator.

tools.name: Scriptable (EasyHDL) generator
tools.description: A generator whose output is produced by an EasyHDL script - Labcenter's BASIC-like hardware description language - instead of a fixed shape. The script assigns the output (OUT = value / OUT = 0 or 1), waits with SLEEP FOR <time> or WAIT UNTIL <condition>, and can use variables, DATA/READ tables, FOR/NEXT, WHILE/WEND, IF/THEN/ELSE/ENDIF, GOTO labels and expressions, so protocol frames (RC5 IR, Manchester, custom serial), swept or random stimuli and closed-loop test benches can be generated without a second microcontroller.
tools.usage: Generator Mode > 'Script' > edit > type the script body (the generator supplies the *SCRIPT GENERATOR wrapper); or place a text script block *SCRIPT GENERATOR <name> ... *ENDSCRIPT and reference it

parameters.name: OUT
parameters.description: The generator's output value (analogue volts or digital 0/1).

parameters.name: SLEEP FOR / WAIT UNTIL
parameters.description: Timing statements; SLEEP advances simulation time, WAIT blocks until a pin/node condition.

parameters.name: FLOAT / INT / NODE / PIN declarations
parameters.description: Variables and references to schematic nodes or pins the script reads.

tools.example:
FLOAT bit = 1.778m
FLOAT half = bit / 2
FOR i = 0 TO 13
  IF (frame & (1 << (13-i))) THEN
    OUT = 0 : SLEEP FOR half : OUT = 1 : SLEEP FOR half
  ELSE
    OUT = 1 : SLEEP FOR half : OUT = 0 : SLEEP FOR half
  ENDIF
NEXT i
tools.notes: EasyHDL is part of the standard simulator (no extra licence); scripts can also define whole components (*SCRIPT PROGRAM) that read NODE/PIN values. Syntax errors are reported in the Simulation Log at netlist time.

tools.name: *SCRIPT ... *ENDSCRIPT (EasyHDL text script block)
tools.description: A text script placed on the schematic (Text Script Mode) whose first line is *SCRIPT GENERATOR <name> or *SCRIPT PROGRAM <name> and last line *ENDSCRIPT. GENERATOR scripts drive a single output used by a scriptable generator; PROGRAM scripts are free-running behavioural models that declare NODE and PIN variables bound to schematic nets and can read and drive several of them - effectively a quick custom model without the VSM SDK. Digital scripts must SLEEP or WAIT to let assigned outputs take effect.
tools.usage:
Text Script Mode > place > type:
*SCRIPT PROGRAM MYMON
NODE clk = CLK
PIN out = U1.RB0
...
*ENDSCRIPT

parameters.name: NODE name = <net>
parameters.description: Binds a variable to a net voltage/logic state.

parameters.name: PIN name = <ref.pin>
parameters.description: Binds a variable to a component pin so it can be read or driven.

parameters.name: PRINT
parameters.description: Writes to the Simulation Log for tracing.

tools.example:
*SCRIPT PROGRAM WATCHDOG
NODE sig = SDA
WHILE 1
  WAIT UNTIL sig = 0
  PRINT "SDA low at ", TIME
  WAIT UNTIL sig = 1
WEND
*ENDSCRIPT
tools.notes: A companion EasyHDL editor/debugger is available from the script's context menu. Analogue scripts read node voltages as floats; digital ones read logic states.

tools.name: System Scope (live-probe oscilloscope)
tools.description: The Proteus 9 interactive oscilloscope: a four-channel scope with X-Y mode, voltage gains from 20V/div down to 2mV/div, timebases from 200ms/div to 0.5us/div, AC/DC coupling per channel, auto and one-shot triggering and cursor measurements. Unlike the classic instrument it uses live probes that are placed and re-positioned on the schematic while the simulation runs, and it docks at the bottom of the window with the other instruments.
tools.usage: Virtual Instruments Mode > 'System Scope' (or the scope icon on the animation bar) > click probes onto wires during simulation; adjust channel gain/timebase/trigger on the docked panel

parameters.name: Channels A-D
parameters.description: Gain, coupling, position, invert per channel.

parameters.name: Timebase / Trigger
parameters.description: Sweep speed, trigger source, level, edge, auto/one-shot.

parameters.name: Cursors
parameters.description: Delta-time and delta-voltage measurements on the frozen trace.

tools.example: Run a PWM motor drive, drop probe A on the PWM pin and B on the motor current-sense resistor, set 100us/div and trigger on A rising to compare phase.
tools.notes: Introduced with the Proteus 9.0 framework; the legacy OSCILLOSCOPE part with wired channels is still available for older projects. Requires the interactive simulator (VSM or Advanced Simulation).

tools.name: CAN Bus Analyser (virtual instrument)
tools.description: Protocol analyser for the CAN models: it captures and timestamps every frame on CANH/CANL, decodes IDs and signals by name from a loaded DBC database, transmits frames on demand (single or periodic) and can inject faults (bit errors, missing ACK, bus-off) to exercise error handling. It supports classical CAN and CAN FD alongside the MCP2515/MCP2518FD controllers and the vehicle ECU node models.
tools.usage: Virtual Instruments Mode > 'CAN Bus Analyser' > CANH/CANL to the bus > edit: bit rate, DBC file; during simulation use the Transmit and Fault tabs

parameters.name: Bit rate / FD data rate
parameters.description: Must match the controller configuration.

parameters.name: DBC file
parameters.description: Signal database for symbolic decode.

parameters.name: Transmit list
parameters.description: Frames to send once or cyclically.

tools.example: Load vehicle.dbc, run, and see 'EngineRPM = 2450' decoded from the Engine ECU node while your MCP2515 firmware requests it.
tools.notes: Included with the VSM licences (CAN technology page); the analyser can act as a passive monitor or an active node.

tools.name: Active Popup
tools.description: A rectangle drawn on the schematic (Active Popup mode) that defines a region to be shown as a live, interactive window inside VSM Studio while the simulation runs. Displays, buttons, pots and sensors inside the region can be watched and clicked from the source-code debugger without switching tabs, and several popups dock on the right of the IDE.
tools.usage: Schematic > Active Popup icon (left toolbar) > drag a box around the area; edit it to name/size the popup; the popups appear when the simulation starts and VSM Studio is active

parameters.name: Region
parameters.description: Schematic area to mirror; can only be created/edited while the simulation is stopped.

parameters.name: Name
parameters.description: Title shown on the docked window.

tools.example: Popups on the LCD, the mode button and POT-HG: single-step the ADC ISR in VSM Studio and turn the pot in the popup between steps.
tools.notes: When popups exist Proteus switches to VSM Studio at simulation start; delete them when you want the schematic tab in front. Popups can be resized while running but not created.

tools.name: Debug > Run Simulation with Timed Breakpoint
tools.description: Starts (or continues) the interactive simulation and pauses it automatically at a specified simulation time, so a design can be advanced to an exact instant - just before an event of interest - and then single-stepped. It is the time-domain counterpart of a source breakpoint and works in both the schematic and Visual Designer.
tools.usage: Debug > Run Simulation with Timed Breakpoint > enter the stop time (e.g. 1.25s) > OK

parameters.name: Breakpoint time
parameters.description: Absolute simulation time at which to pause.

tools.example: Set 2.000s to land just before a 2-second timer overflow, then Step Into the ISR when it fires.
tools.notes: The Debug menu also offers plain 'Run Simulation' (F12) and a run that ignores breakpoints; the status bar shows the simulated time while paused.

tools.name: Debug > Animated Single Step
tools.description: Runs the firmware one instruction/line at a time at a slow, visible rate so the execution path can be watched moving through the source or the flowchart (decision branches, loop bodies) while the schematic animates in step. It is a quick way to spot wrong branches without setting individual breakpoints.
tools.usage: Pause the simulation > Debug > Animated Single Step (toggle); stop with Pause or Stop

parameters.name: Step rate
parameters.description: Governed by the Single Step Time in Animation Options.

tools.example: In a Visual Designer nightlight flowchart, animate stepping to see the decision block take the NO branch when lux > 100.
tools.notes: Regular stepping uses Step Over (F10) and Step Into (F11) from the source window toolbar.

tools.name: Debug > Step Over / Step Into / Step Out / Run To
tools.description: The source-level stepping commands available when the simulation is paused: Step Over (F10) executes one line, treating a call as a unit; Step Into (F11) enters the called routine; Step Out runs until the current routine returns; Run To executes until the line under the cursor is reached (Visual Designer offers 'Step to' on a block's context menu). Each step advances simulation time by the instructions executed and propagates their effects through the circuit before pausing again.
tools.usage: Pause > Debug menu (or the icons at the top of the source window) > Step Over (F10) / Step Into (F11) / Step Out / Run To; right-click a source line > Run to cursor

parameters.name: Disassembly view
parameters.description: Right-click the source > Disassembly to step at instruction level with the same commands.

tools.example: Break on the button-release handler, F11 into lcd_puts(), F10 across the busy-wait, then Step Out back to main.
tools.notes: Capacitors do not discharge and motors keep their state while paused - the whole system is under time control.

tools.name: Watchpoint conditions (Watch Window breakpoints)
tools.description: Conditional breakpoints attached to Watch Window items: right-click an item and set a watchpoint condition (equal, not equal, less/greater, bit masks) and the simulation pauses when the register or variable meets it - even during free-running simulation, since the Watch Window is the one debug window that updates live. Multiple items can be combined, and conditions are switched off from the same dialogue.
tools.usage: Debug > Watch Window > right-click > Add items by name (or from the Variables window 'Add to Watch Window') > right-click item > Watchpoint condition > set operator/value > OK

parameters.name: Item
parameters.description: SFR/register (by name) or C variable (by address).

parameters.name: Condition
parameters.description: Comparison and value; display format (hex/binary/decimal) per item.

tools.example: ADRESH == 0x01 AND ADRESL <= 0xFF pauses the F1 evaluation-board firmware as the POT passes mid-scale on the way down.
tools.notes: Variables are tracked by address, so re-add them after recompiling if the compiler relocated them. 'Turn off watchpoints' disables all conditions at once.

tools.name: Real Time Breakpoint (probe hardware breakpoint)
tools.description: A voltage or current probe configured to pause the simulation when a hardware condition occurs: a digital breakpoint on a logic level or edge, or an analogue breakpoint when the value crosses a threshold, optionally with an arm time before which it is ignored. It traps events that firmware breakpoints cannot express - the first activity on an I2C line, an over-current, a glitch - and drops you into the source at the instruction that caused it.
tools.usage: Voltage Probe Mode > place on the wire > edit > Real Time Breakpoint: Digital (trigger value 0/1) or Analogue (threshold, direction) > Arm time

parameters.name: Breakpoint type
parameters.description: Disabled / Digital / Analogue.

parameters.name: Trigger value / threshold
parameters.description: Logic level or voltage/current level.

parameters.name: Arm time
parameters.description: Simulation time before which the breakpoint is inactive.

tools.example: Probe on SDA, digital breakpoint trigger 0, arm time 1s: the simulation pauses inside the I2C start routine when temperature mode is entered.
tools.notes: Probes are removed from the schematic when debugging is finished; they do not affect the circuit.

tools.name: Debug > Configure Diagnostics (Diagnostic Control System)
tools.description: The tracing facility of the simulator: per-model diagnostic categories (for a CPU, e.g. instruction execution, interrupts, timers, UART, I2C/SPI, memory access; for peripherals, their own event classes) can be enabled at a chosen level and, optionally, only between start and stop times. Enabled categories write timestamped messages to the Simulation Log, giving an execution trace without instrumenting the firmware.
tools.usage: Debug > Configure Diagnostics > expand the model (e.g. U1 PIC16F877A) > tick categories > set trace level and optional time window > OK; view results in the Simulation Log

parameters.name: Category / level
parameters.description: Which events and how verbose (Disabled, Warnings only, Full trace).

parameters.name: Start / stop time
parameters.description: Limits tracing to a window to keep the log readable.

tools.example: Enable 'MSSP I2C' full trace on the PIC between 1.2s and 1.4s to log every start/ACK/byte during the temperature read.
tools.notes: All processor models are 'fully integrated into the Proteus Diagnostic Control System' per the technical specifications. Full tracing slows simulation dramatically - use the time window.

tools.name: Debug > Reset Popup Windows
tools.description: Restores all debug and instrument popup windows (CPU register, memory, watch, peripheral windows, instrument panels) to their default positions and sizes. Use it after windows have been dragged off-screen or closed in a multi-monitor session, or when a layout saved in the project no longer fits the display.
tools.usage: Debug > Reset Popup Windows
tools.example: After moving a project from a two-monitor workstation to a laptop, the I2C debugger window is off-screen: Debug > Reset Popup Windows brings it back.
tools.notes: Window positions are stored in the project; this command only resets layout, not data.

tools.name: Debug > Reset Persistent Model Data
tools.description: Clears the data that some models keep between simulation runs - EEPROM and flash memory contents, MMC card images written by firmware, non-volatile digital-pot wipers, RTC time and similar 'persistent model data' - returning them to their initial-contents properties. Use it to guarantee a clean first-power-up test after firmware has written configuration or logs to non-volatile devices.
tools.usage: Debug > Reset Persistent Model Data (simulation stopped)
tools.example: Firmware stores a calibration flag in a 24LC256; to re-test the 'first boot' path, stop, Reset Persistent Model Data, and run again.
tools.notes: Persistence is what lets a data-logger design keep its records across runs; reset only when that is not wanted.

tools.name: Debug > Use Remote Debug Monitor
tools.description: Enables the remote debug server so an external IDE (MPLAB X / MPLAB 8 via the Proteus VSM debugger plug-in, Atmel/Microchip Studio, Keil uVision, IAR, or a GDB client such as STM32CubeIDE from 9.2) can drive the Proteus simulation as its debug target: the IDE controls run/step/breakpoints and reads variables while Proteus animates the circuit. It is the switch that has to be on before the IDE's debugger can connect.
tools.usage: Debug > Use Remote Debug Monitor (tick); then in the IDE select the Proteus VSM debugger/GDB target and start a debug session

parameters.name: Host / port
parameters.description: Connection settings for the external debugger (local machine by default).

tools.example: MPLAB X > Project Properties > Hardware Tool 'Proteus VSM Viewer' > Debug Main Project: Proteus opens the design and stops at main() when MPLAB breaks.
tools.notes: The Program File on the MCU must be the same image the IDE built. The MPLAB plug-in and IDE driver installers are on the Labcenter downloads page.

tools.name: Debug > CPU debug windows (Registers, Source Code, Program/Data Memory, EEPROM, Stack, peripheral windows)
tools.description: The per-processor windows added to the Debug menu when a simulation is paused, named after the instance (e.g. 'PIC CPU Registers - U1', 'PIC CPU Program Memory', 'PIC CPU Data Memory', 'PIC CPU EEPROM Memory', 'PIC CPU Stack', 'PIC CPU Source Code', plus SFR/peripheral views such as USART, I2C, SPI, timers and ports), and equivalent windows for peripheral models that expose memory (EEPROMs, LCD RAM). They refresh on every pause/step and can be tiled or cascaded from the same menu.
tools.usage: Pause the simulation > Debug > choose the window (e.g. 'PIC CPU Data Memory - U1'); Debug > Tile Horizontally / Tile Vertically / Cascade to arrange

parameters.name: Display format
parameters.description: Right-click to change radix or width where supported.

tools.example: Open 'AVR CPU Registers' and 'AVR SRAM' while stepping an ISR to confirm SREG and the stack pointer are restored.
tools.notes: Closed windows reopen from the Debug menu; only the Watch Window updates during free-running simulation.

tools.name: Frames per Second (Animation Options)
tools.description: The screen refresh rate of an interactive simulation, set in System > Set Animation Options. Default 20 frames per second gives smooth animation without overloading the display; lower it on slow graphics or very busy schematics, raise it to 25 for smoother meters and terminals. It does not change how much simulated time elapses per second - that is Timestep per Frame.
tools.usage: System > Set Animation Options > Simulation Speed > Frames per Second

parameters.name: Frames per Second
parameters.description: Integer refresh rate (default 20).

tools.example: Set 25fps so a Virtual Terminal streaming text feels real-time; combine with a 40ms timestep to keep one second of simulation per second of wall time.
tools.notes: Frames per Second x Timestep per Frame = simulated seconds per real second when the PC can keep up; the status bar shows the achieved CPU load.

tools.name: Timestep per Frame (Animation Options)
tools.description: The amount of simulation time advanced during each animation frame (default 50ms at 20fps = real time). Reducing it slows fast circuits so their behaviour can be watched (e.g. 10ms or 20ms per frame runs at 1/5 or 2/5 real time); increasing it makes slow circuits (RTC, thermal) run faster than real time if the CPU has headroom.
tools.usage: System > Set Animation Options > Simulation Speed > Timestep per Frame

parameters.name: Timestep per Frame
parameters.description: Simulation time per frame, e.g. 50m, 10m.

tools.example: Watch a 1kHz PWM edge sequence on animated pins by setting 20us per frame.
tools.notes: If the simulation cannot keep up, the frame rate drops rather than the timestep; the CPU-load indicator on the status bar shows this.

tools.name: Single Step Time (Animation Options)
tools.description: How much simulation time elapses for each press of the Step button on the animation control panel (and for Animated Single Step) when no processor is being stepped at source level. It lets analogue/digital circuits without an MCU be advanced in controlled increments.
tools.usage: System > Set Animation Options > Simulation Speed > Single Step Time

parameters.name: Single Step Time
parameters.description: Time per Step press, e.g. 50m or 1u.

tools.example: Set 1us and press Step repeatedly to walk a 555 astable through one charge cycle on the animated LED.
tools.notes: With a microcontroller in the design, source stepping takes precedence when the Source Code tab is active.

tools.name: Max SPICE Timestep (Animation Options)
tools.description: Upper bound on the analogue simulator's internal timestep during interactive simulation. Lowering it (e.g. to 1us) forces finer resolution for fast analogue edges - often the cure for 'high-frequency' simulation errors or missed PWM detail - at the cost of speed; leaving it large lets slow circuits run quickly.
tools.usage: System > Set Animation Options > Simulation Speed > Max SPICE Timestep

parameters.name: Max SPICE Timestep
parameters.description: Maximum analogue step, e.g. 25m (default) or 1u.

tools.example: A 100kHz switching converter shows jagged waveforms on the scope: set Max SPICE Timestep to 100n.
tools.notes: For graph-based analyses the equivalent is the TMAX/maximum step in the graph's SPICE options.

tools.name: Animation display options (Show Voltage & Current on Probes, Show Logic State of Pins, Show Wire Voltage by Colour, Show Wire Current with Arrows)
tools.description: The check boxes in Set Animation Options that control the visual feedback during interactive simulation: probe readouts on placed probes, coloured logic-state squares on pins (red/blue/grey for high/low/floating), wire colouring by voltage (red positive through green to blue negative, scaled by the Maximum Voltage setting) and current-direction arrows on wires above the Current Threshold. They are what make the schematic 'live' and are turned off for speed on large designs.
tools.usage: System > Set Animation Options > Animation Options section > tick/untick; Voltage/Current Ranges: Maximum Voltage, Current Threshold

parameters.name: Maximum Voltage
parameters.description: Full-scale for wire colour mapping (default 6V).

parameters.name: Current Threshold
parameters.description: Minimum current for arrows (default 1uA).

tools.example: Teaching a divider circuit: enable wire voltage colouring and current arrows so students see the potential gradient and current direction.
tools.notes: The SPICE Options button on this dialogue opens the same Simulator Options as System > Set Simulator Options.

tools.name: SPICE tolerances (RELTOL, ABSTOL, VNTOL, CHGTOL)
tools.description: The convergence tolerances of the ProSPICE (SPICE3F5) kernel, edited on the Tolerances tab of System > Set Simulator Options (or per graph from its SPICE Options): RELTOL relative error (default 0.001), ABSTOL absolute current error (1pA), VNTOL absolute voltage error (1uV) and CHGTOL charge tolerance (10fC). Loosening RELTOL to 0.01 trades accuracy for speed and often resolves 'timestep too small' failures in switching circuits; tightening them improves precision for low-level analogue work.
tools.usage: System > Set Simulator Options > Tolerances tab > edit values > OK (per-graph: Edit Graph > SPICE Options)

parameters.name: RELTOL
parameters.description: Relative accuracy of voltages/currents (0.001 default).

parameters.name: ABSTOL / VNTOL
parameters.description: Absolute current / voltage error floors.

parameters.name: CHGTOL
parameters.description: Charge tolerance for capacitors.

tools.example: A boost converter fails at 300us with 'timestep too small': set RELTOL 0.01 and ABSTOL 1n, re-run, then tighten again once the topology is right.
tools.notes: Global defaults apply to interactive simulation; graphs can override them. See the convergence troubleshooting entry for the diagnostic sequence.

tools.name: GMIN and GMIN stepping (Simulator Options)
tools.description: GMIN is the minimum conductance the simulator places across every semiconductor junction (default 1e-12 S) to keep the matrix non-singular; GMIN stepping is the DC operating-point strategy that starts with a large conductance and steps it down to the final value when a direct Newton solution fails. Raising GMIN (1e-10) or increasing the number of GMIN steps helps circuits with floating nodes, back-to-back diodes or high-impedance gates find an operating point.
tools.usage: System > Set Simulator Options > Tolerances / Iteration tab > GMIN, GMIN Steps (and Source Steps for source stepping)

parameters.name: GMIN
parameters.description: Minimum junction conductance.

parameters.name: GMIN steps / Source steps
parameters.description: Number of continuation steps tried before giving up on the DC solution.

tools.example: 'Singular matrix' at t=0 in an op-amp integrator: raise GMIN to 1e-10 and add a 100M resistor across the integrating capacitor.
tools.notes: A floating node warning in the Simulation Log usually points to the real cause - fix the schematic before tuning GMIN.

tools.name: Integration method and iteration limits (Gear / Trapezoidal, ITL1, ITL2, ITL4, TRTOL)
tools.description: Transient-analysis controls in Simulator Options: the numerical integration method (Trapezoidal - default, more accurate but can ring numerically; Gear - more damped and stable for stiff switching circuits, at some cost in speed) with its maximum order, the Newton iteration limits ITL1 (DC operating point, default 100), ITL2 (DC transfer curve) and ITL4 (per transient timepoint, default 10), and TRTOL, the truncation-error factor that scales the automatic timestep.
tools.usage: System > Set Simulator Options > Iteration / Transient tabs > Integration Method (Gear or Trapezoidal), Max Order, ITL1/ITL2/ITL4, TRTOL

parameters.name: Integration method
parameters.description: TRAPEZOIDAL or GEAR.

parameters.name: ITL1 / ITL2 / ITL4
parameters.description: Iteration limits for operating point, DC sweep and transient steps.

parameters.name: TRTOL
parameters.description: Truncation tolerance (default 7).

tools.example: A flyback converter's waveform oscillates numerically at each switching edge: switch to Gear integration and raise ITL4 to 50.
tools.notes: Gear generally converges to a more stable solution at the expense of run time; keep Trapezoidal for oscillators and resonant circuits where damping distorts results.

tools.name: Digital simulator (DSIM) timing options (propagation delay mode, random delay, glitch handling)
tools.description: The DSIM tab of Simulator Options controls how digital primitives time their outputs: whether typical, minimum or maximum datasheet propagation delays are used, whether an optional random spread is applied to delays to expose race conditions, how zero-width glitches are treated, and the default timing used by primitives that lack explicit delay properties. Mixed-mode interface behaviour (logic thresholds, rise/fall times of the analogue-to-digital bridges) is set alongside.
tools.usage: System > Set Simulator Options > DSIM tab > Propagation Delay (Typical/Minimum/Maximum), Random Delay Spread, glitch options

parameters.name: Delay selection
parameters.description: Typ/min/max for library logic families.

parameters.name: Random delay
parameters.description: Percentage spread to reveal timing-sensitive logic.

tools.example: A ripple counter decoded with gates works with typical delays but glitches with maximum delays - the Digital graph shows the hazard the hardware will exhibit.
tools.notes: Per-instance delays can be overridden with the digital primitive timing properties (TDLH/TDHL style) on the component.

tools.name: Edit Graph properties (Start time, Stop time, Initial DC solution, Always simulate, Log netlist(s), SPICE Options)
tools.description: The dialogue opened by right-clicking a graph > Edit Properties (or Graph > Edit Graph) that sets the analysis window and options: Start time and Stop time (default 0-1s), the left/right axis labels, 'Initial DC solution' (compute the operating point before the transient, untick to start from zero-state), 'Always simulate' (re-run even if nothing changed), 'Log netlist(s)' (write the SDF netlist to the log for inspection) and a SPICE Options button for per-graph tolerances. Sweep-type graphs (DC/AC Sweep) add the swept variable name, start/stop values and number of steps.
tools.usage: Right-click the graph > Edit Properties > set Start time / Stop time etc. > OK; Graph > Simulate Graph (Space) to run

parameters.name: Start time / Stop time
parameters.description: Transient window; results before Start are simulated but not stored.

parameters.name: Initial DC solution
parameters.description: Operating-point pre-solve on/off.

parameters.name: Sweep variable / Start / Stop / Steps
parameters.description: DC and AC Sweep graphs only (e.g. X from 100k to 5M in 10 steps).

tools.example: I2C traffic graph: Start time 1s, Stop time 2s skips the initialisation chatter; the DPulse at 1.25s then triggers the read.
tools.notes: Simulation always begins at t=0 regardless of Start time; only display/storage is windowed. Type '100u' and Proteus converts to 100E-6.

tools.name: Graph > Add Trace (probes, generators and trace expressions)
tools.description: Adds a trace to the current graph: with probes/generators tagged it offers to add them in one step (Quick Add), otherwise the Add Transient/Frequency/... Trace dialogue lets you pick a probe for the left or right axis and, importantly, enter a trace expression combining probes (P1, P2, P3, P4 stand for the selected probes) with arithmetic and functions - e.g. P1-P2 for a differential voltage, P1*P2 for instantaneous power, or functions such as ABS(), SQRT(), LOG(), SIN(), EXP() and the transient/frequency-specific operators. Dragging a probe onto the graph is the shortcut for a plain trace.
tools.usage: Select the graph > Graph > Add Trace (or right-click graph > Add Trace) > Name, Probe P1..P4, Expression, Axis (Left/Right) > OK

parameters.name: Probe P1-P4
parameters.description: Up to four probes/generators referenced by the expression.

parameters.name: Expression
parameters.description: Arithmetic on P1..P4 with built-in functions.

parameters.name: Axis
parameters.description: Left or right Y axis (each auto-scaled separately).

tools.example: Expression P1*P2 with P1 = VOUT probe and P2 = IOUT current probe plots instantaneous load power on the right axis.
tools.notes: Trace expressions are evaluated after simulation, so they cost nothing at run time. Digital graphs take logic probes only (no expressions).

tools.name: Graph > Simulate Graph (Space)
tools.description: Runs the analysis defined by the current graph (the one marked on the Graph menu, or the selected/maximised one) and redraws its traces when the kernel finishes: the schematic is netlisted to SDF, the ProSPICE/DSIM/CPU models execute from t=0 to the Stop time or until quiescent, and progress is shown on the status bar. Esc aborts a running simulation; the Simulation Log holds warnings and the netlist if logging was enabled.
tools.usage: Select or maximise the graph > Graph > Simulate Graph, or press the space bar; right-click graph > Simulate
tools.example: Change R2 to 4k7, press Space, and the Frequency graph updates to show the new cut-off; press Space again after adding a current probe to plot its trace.
tools.notes: Interactive controls (buttons, pots) cannot be used during a graph simulation - use generators as stimuli. The Simulation Advisor icon opens the log if warnings occurred.

tools.name: Graph > Maximise, Zoom to Area and graph toolbar
tools.description: Opens the selected graph in its own tab (right-click > Maximise, or double-click the title) where the graph toolbar and menus replace the schematic ones: Zoom to Area (drag a box, or Shift+drag on the graph), Zoom in/out/fit, cursor toggles, Export Graph Data (CSV/text), Print Graph and the trace list. Maximising is required for accurate cursor measurements and to read fine detail such as single I2C sequences.
tools.usage: Right-click graph > Maximise (new tab) > toolbar 'Zoom to area' icon > drag a rectangle; Shift+drag also zooms; close the tab to return to the schematic

parameters.name: Zoom to Area
parameters.description: Rectangular zoom on both axes.

parameters.name: Cursors
parameters.description: Left/right mouse cursors read time and value; delta shown on the status bar.

tools.example: Maximise the digital I2C graph and zoom repeatedly on 1.25-1.26s until one start-address-ACK sequence fills the tab.
tools.notes: The right axis may be scaled differently from the left - check the axis labels before comparing trace amplitudes.

tools.name: Frequency / Noise graph reference generator and Log Spectral Contributions
tools.description: Small-signal analyses need an input reference: a generator dragged onto the Frequency, Noise or AC Sweep graph defines the input node (its amplitude is irrelevant, the analysis is linearised about the operating point). Frequency graphs plot magnitude (left axis, dB) and phase (right axis); Noise graphs plot output noise per root-hertz at each probe and input-referred noise for the reference, and the 'Log Spectral Contributions' option on the Edit Noise Graph dialogue lists the noise of every element (op-amp internals prefixed U1_ etc.) in the Simulation Log under 'Total Noise Contributions'.
tools.usage: Place a Frequency or Noise graph > drag the input generator onto it (becomes the reference) > drag probes > Edit Properties: start/stop frequency, points per decade, (Noise) Log Spectral Contributions > Space

parameters.name: Reference generator
parameters.description: Generator defining the input for the sweep.

parameters.name: Start / Stop frequency, Interval
parameters.description: Sweep range and decade/linear spacing.

parameters.name: Log Spectral Contributions
parameters.description: Noise graph option for per-element breakdown.

tools.example: Op-amp bandpass: Frequency graph 10Hz-100kHz shows -90 degree phase at the extremes; Noise graph with contributions logged reveals R1 dominates the output noise.
tools.notes: Current probes are ignored in noise analysis. Frequency analysis models are linear - saturation and slew rate do not appear.

tools.name: Simulation Log (netlist, warnings and diagnostics viewer)
tools.description: The log kept for the last simulation, opened by clicking the Simulation Advisor icon at the bottom of the schematic frame (or Debug > Simulation Log): it lists netlist compilation messages, model resolution (which SPICEMODEL/MODFILE was loaded), convergence warnings with the offending node and time, timing-violation reports from peripheral models, diagnostic trace output, noise contribution tables and EasyHDL PRINT statements. It is the first place to look when a simulation behaves unexpectedly.
tools.usage: Click the Simulation Advisor icon (bottom-left) or Debug > Simulation Log; during interactive simulation it opens in the VSM Studio tab
tools.example: 'Model file BIPOLAR.MDF not found' or 'Timestep too small at t=3.1e-4' in the log identifies a library-path or convergence problem immediately.
tools.notes: Tick 'Log netlist(s)' in the graph properties to include the SDF netlist; enable Configure Diagnostics categories for traces.
